Digging into southern Trinidad’s forgotten heritage

by

Radhica De Silva
15 hours ago
20261026

Member of the Researching the Environment through Archaeology and Community Heritage (REACH) project.

Members of the Researching the Environment through Archaeology and Community Heritage (REACH) project team.

PHOTOS COURTESY DR SHAD GOBINSINGH

Member of the Researching the Environment through Archaeology and Community Heritage (REACH) project.

PHOTOS COURTESY DR SHAD GOBINSINGH

Member of the Researching the Environment through Archaeology and Community Heritage (REACH) project.

RAD­HI­CA DE SIL­VA

Se­nior Mul­ti­me­dia Re­porter

rad­hi­ca.sookraj@guardian.co.tt

Listen to audio version of this article

0:00 / 4:17
Instaread

South­ern Trinidad’s for­got­ten his­to­ry is be­ing brought to light through ar­chae­o­log­i­cal re­search that is un­cov­er­ing ev­i­dence of the lives of In­dige­nous peo­ple, in­den­tured labour­ers and the com­mu­ni­ties they built, while train­ing a new gen­er­a­tion of lo­cal re­searchers to pre­serve the coun­try’s her­itage.

Dr Shad Gob­ins­ingh, Field Di­rec­tor of the Re­search­ing the En­vi­ron­ment through Ar­chae­ol­o­gy and Com­mu­ni­ty Her­itage (REACH) project, said the in­ter­na­tion­al ar­chae­o­log­i­cal field school was help­ing to ad­dress gaps in re­search on south­ern Trinidad while equip­ping uni­ver­si­ty stu­dents with prac­ti­cal skills to in­ves­ti­gate and pre­serve the coun­try’s past.

Speak­ing ex­clu­sive­ly to Guardian Me­dia, Dr Gob­ins­ingh said the 2026 field school rep­re­sent­ed an im­por­tant step in de­vel­op­ing lo­cal ex­per­tise in ar­chae­ol­o­gy and her­itage con­ser­va­tion.

“So we are here for two rea­sons, first to equip a new gen­er­a­tion of grad­u­ates with es­sen­tial hands-on field tech­niques, from ex­ca­va­tion, sur­vey­ing, tran­sects and map­ping, to metic­u­lous preser­va­tion and con­ser­va­tion of the arte­facts,” he said.

The sec­ond ob­jec­tive, he ex­plained, was to un­cov­er sto­ries that had re­mained large­ly un­doc­u­ment­ed.

“We want to un­cov­er the hid­den sto­ries of our past that gen­er­al­ly go un­told for far too long,” Dr Gob­ins­ingh said.

He added that South­ern Trinidad re­mains an area that is large­ly un­der-re­searched.

“This field school of­fers op­por­tu­ni­ty to con­duct ground­break­ing re­search, men­tor stu­dents and pro­vide the pub­lic with a deep­er and more mean­ing­ful un­der­stand­ing of the is­land’s ear­ly in­hab­i­tants.”

He said the REACH project be­gan its first field sea­son in 2025, fo­cus­ing on Palmiste Park, Puz­zle Is­land and Pood­hai La­goon. Its sec­ond field sea­son re­turned to Palmiste Park in Au­gust 2026, with field­work con­duct­ed from Au­gust 10 to 22 and lab­o­ra­to­ry train­ing at The Uni­ver­si­ty of the West In­dies (UWI), St Au­gus­tine.

“The project brings to­geth­er the Na­tion­al Trust of Trinidad and To­ba­go, UWI and North­west­ern Uni­ver­si­ty in Chica­go, with sup­port from lo­cal part­ners in­clud­ing the Pe­nal/Debe Re­gion­al Cor­po­ra­tion and the Palmiste His­tor­i­cal So­ci­ety,” he said.

Led in­ter­na­tion­al­ly by Dr Mark Hauser of North­west­ern Uni­ver­si­ty, the ini­tia­tive com­bines ar­chae­o­log­i­cal ex­ca­va­tion with archival re­search, oral his­to­ries and knowl­edge shared by res­i­dents to ex­am­ine how peo­ple lived, worked and es­tab­lished com­mu­ni­ties across south­ern Trinidad.

Re­search dur­ing the 2025 field sea­son demon­strat­ed the ar­chae­o­log­i­cal po­ten­tial of these land­scapes, doc­u­ment­ing ma­te­r­i­al as­so­ci­at­ed with the his­toric es­tate and its labour­ing com­mu­ni­ties at Palmiste Park, along­side ev­i­dence point­ing to a much longer In­dige­nous his­to­ry, he not­ed.

The find­ings are sig­nif­i­cant, Gob­ins­ingh said, be­cause the project ex­am­ines the his­to­ry of in­den­ture­ship and the post-in­den­ture­ship pe­ri­od be­yond the for­mal sys­tem of labour, look­ing at how peo­ple built homes, cul­ti­vat­ed land, man­aged wa­ter, prac­tised re­li­gion and de­vel­oped a sense of be­long­ing.

Dr Gob­ins­ingh not­ed that the col­lab­o­ra­tion of re­searchers and her­itage pro­fes­sion­als was es­sen­tial to ad­vanc­ing this work and pro­tect­ing ar­chae­o­log­i­cal sites for fu­ture gen­er­a­tions.

The project al­so draws on the ex­pe­ri­ences of peo­ple who con­tin­ue to live in these his­toric land­scapes. At Pood­hai La­goon and Su­chit Trace, Pe­nal, re­searchers have en­gaged res­i­dents in con­ver­sa­tions about set­tle­ment pat­terns, farm­ing prac­tices and changes in the sur­round­ing en­vi­ron­ment, he added.

Dr Gob­ins­ingh said oral his­to­ries have helped doc­u­ment the cul­ti­va­tion of rice, lentils, bo­di and oth­er crops, as well as the re­la­tion­ship be­tween hous­es, agri­cul­tur­al fields and wa­ter sources. Res­i­dents have al­so shared ac­counts of flood­ing and re­lo­ca­tion that in­flu­enced how com­mu­ni­ties de­vel­oped.

This ap­proach places lo­cal res­i­dents at the cen­tre of the re­search, recog­nis­ing that their mem­o­ries and knowl­edge can help ar­chae­ol­o­gists in­ter­pret the phys­i­cal ev­i­dence found in the land­scape.

More on REACH

The field school al­so gives UWI His­to­ry stu­dents op­por­tu­ni­ties to gain prac­ti­cal ex­pe­ri­ence in his­tor­i­cal ar­chae­ol­o­gy, a dis­ci­pline that us­es ma­te­r­i­al re­mains and doc­u­men­tary ev­i­dence to un­der­stand past lives.

Stu­dents re­ceive train­ing in ar­chae­o­log­i­cal sur­vey­ing, ex­ca­va­tion, record­ing, map­ping, arte­fact pro­cess­ing and in­ter­pre­ta­tion, work­ing along­side prac­tis­ing ar­chae­ol­o­gists and her­itage pro­fes­sion­als.

The pro­gramme is in­tend­ed to con­tin­ue over sev­er­al years, al­low­ing suc­ces­sive groups of stu­dents to con­tribute to orig­i­nal re­search while de­vel­op­ing skills that are not typ­i­cal­ly ac­quired through class­room in­struc­tion alone.

Dr Gob­ins­ingh said the ul­ti­mate ob­jec­tive was to strength­en the coun­try’s abil­i­ty to safe­guard its ar­chae­o­log­i­cal and her­itage re­sources.

Through con­tin­ued re­search, train­ing and com­mu­ni­ty par­tic­i­pa­tion, Dr Gob­ins­ingh said REACH aims to build a stronger un­der­stand­ing of south­ern Trinidad’s past and en­sure that the his­to­ries of the peo­ple who shaped its land­scapes are doc­u­ment­ed and pre­served.
